title: Hidden in Plain Sight
subtitle: Steganography — LSB Detection
narrative: After the DNS tunnel was shut down (Scenario 04), the DLP and network monitoring teams tightened egress controls. But a sophisticated insider knows that when network channels are watched, the next step is application-layer steganography — hiding data inside files that look completely normal. An insider at Prism Design Inc. is suspected of using exactly this approach to leak product designs. The DLP system caught nothing — no suspicious attachments, no cloud uploads. But a sharp-eyed analyst noticed that the suspect sent three 'cat photos' to an external email address the night before a competitor unveiled a suspiciously similar product. All three PNGs look innocent. Your job: find the one that's hiding something.
learningObjective: Understand LSB (Least Significant Bit) steganography — how data can be hidden in the least significant bits of pixel color values without visually altering an image. Learn to identify steganographic images through statistical analysis, file size anomalies, and EXIF metadata inconsistencies.

preQuiz.question: What is LSB steganography?
options: Encrypting an image file with a password
Hiding data by modifying the least significant bits of pixel color values
Compressing image metadata to reduce file size
Embedding a watermark in the image header
preQuiz.explanation: LSB steganography hides data by replacing the least significant bit of each color channel (R, G, B) in a pixel. Since changing the LSB only alters the color value by 1 (e.g., from 200 to 201), the visual difference is imperceptible to the human eye — but the bits can encode arbitrary data.

preQuiz.question: How does pixel color depth work in a standard 24-bit PNG image?
options: Each pixel has one 24-bit value for brightness
Each pixel has three 8-bit channels (R, G, B), with each channel ranging from 0 to 255
Each pixel stores 24 separate color entries
Color depth only applies to JPEG, not PNG
preQuiz.explanation: In a 24-bit PNG, each pixel has three color channels (Red, Green, Blue), each represented by 8 bits (0-255). This means each pixel carries 24 bits of color data — and an LSB steganography tool can hide 3 bits of secret data per pixel (one bit per channel).

preQuiz.question: Approximately how much data can be hidden in a 1920×1080 image using single-bit LSB steganography across all three color channels?
options: About 8 KB
About 80 KB
About 760 KB
About 6 MB
preQuiz.explanation: A 1920×1080 image has 2,073,600 pixels × 3 channels = 6,220,800 available LSBs. At 1 bit each: 6,220,800 / 8 = 777,600 bytes ≈ 760 KB.

preQuiz.question: What is EXIF metadata in a digital image?
options: The raw pixel data stored in the file
Embedded information about the camera, date, GPS location, and capture settings
A digital signature proving the image has not been modified
The compression algorithm used to reduce file size
preQuiz.explanation: EXIF (Exchangeable Image File Format) metadata records information like camera model, capture date/time, GPS coordinates, and exposure settings. Its absence or inconsistency can be a forensic clue.

hints.text: All three images are the same resolution (1920x1080). Compare their file sizes — one is noticeably larger than the others. Why?

One of the three images has two inconsistencies: its file size doesn't match what you'd expect for the same resolution, and something is missing from its metadata that the other two have. Which image?

The chi-square statistic measures how randomly distributed the least significant bits are across an image. A natural photograph hovers around 1.0 because camera noise is essentially random. When the value drops significantly, it means the LSBs carry structured data instead of random noise. Which specialized analysis tool can extract hidden payloads from PNG images by reading those modified LSBs in sequence?

debriefing.title: How LSB Steganography Works
debriefing.concept: In a 24-bit color image, each pixel has three 8-bit color channels (R, G, B). The least significant bit of each channel contributes the least to the visible color — changing it alters the value by just 1 out of 256. LSB steganography replaces these bits with secret data bits. A 1920×1080 image has ~6.2 million pixels × 3 channels = ~18.6 million bits available, enough to hide ~2.3 MB of data. The visual change is imperceptible, but statistical analysis can detect it: natural images have randomly distributed LSBs (chi-square ≈ 1.0), while stego images show structured patterns (chi-square < 0.7).
debriefing.realWorldTool: Detection tools: zsteg (for PNG), StegDetect, StegExpose, and chi-square statistical tests. StegHide and OpenStego are common embedding tools. RS analysis and chi-square analysis are the primary statistical detection methods.
debriefing.caseConnection: In this case, three clues pointed to cat_03.png: (1) file size 14% larger than expected, (2) EXIF stripped while the other images retained metadata, and (3) LSB chi-square of 0.48 (far below the natural ~0.9). zsteg confirmed a zip archive payload. The steghide log in the Tools folder was the smoking gun.
debriefing.furtherReading: zsteg, StegHide, chi-square analysis for steganalysis, RS analysis, PNG structure and color channels, EXIF metadata forensics

postQuiz.question: What statistical test is commonly used to detect LSB steganography?
options: SHA-256 hash comparison
Chi-square analysis of LSB distribution
CRC32 checksum verification
Entropy measurement of file headers
postQuiz.explanation: Chi-square analysis compares the observed distribution of LSB values against the expected distribution in a natural image. Natural images have near-random LSB patterns (chi-square ≈ 1.0), while LSB steganography creates structured patterns that lower the chi-square value significantly.

postQuiz.question: Why is it suspicious when an image has its EXIF metadata stripped?
options: EXIF removal always indicates steganography
It may indicate the image was processed to remove identifying metadata before embedding hidden data
EXIF can only be removed using forensic tools
Stripped EXIF means the image file is corrupted
postQuiz.explanation: While there are legitimate reasons to strip EXIF (privacy), in a forensic context it's suspicious — especially when other images from the same device retain their EXIF. Stripping EXIF removes timestamps, camera info, and GPS that could help trace the image's origin, and some steganography tools automatically strip it.

postQuiz.question: Why did cat_03.png have its EXIF metadata stripped while cat_01 and cat_02 retained theirs?
options: The image was uploaded to social media, which strips EXIF automatically
The steganography embedding tool (Steghide) stripped EXIF during the embedding process
The camera malfunctioned when taking the third photo
EXIF is only stored in JPEG files, not PNG
postQuiz.explanation: Many steganography tools strip EXIF during embedding because the metadata can conflict with the modified pixel data. The steghide_history.log confirmed: 'EXIF metadata stripped from output.'

postQuiz.question: Why did cat_03.png's LSB chi-square value (0.48) differ so significantly from cat_01 (0.92) and cat_02 (0.89)?
options: cat_03 was taken with a lower-quality camera sensor
The embedded zip archive replaced the natural LSB distribution with structured data, changing the statistical signature
cat_03 used a different color space (CMYK instead of RGB)
PNG compression artifacts lowered the chi-square value
postQuiz.explanation: Natural images have semi-random LSBs (chi-square ≈ 1.0). When a compressed file (like a zip) replaces those LSBs, it introduces structured patterns that significantly lower the chi-square statistic.
